claim: Parameter-based knowledge editing cannot reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities. The near-perfect editing results reported in prior work do not survive realistic evaluation, and the limitation is geometric rather than incidental: localized weight edits are disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space and propagate globally, so damage compounds as edits accumulate. A parameter-free approach that leaves the weights untouched is therefore a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim Can parameter-based knowledge editing reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities?, run a realistic sequential-edit benchmark on public COUNTERFACT and ZSRE using GPT-2 and GPT-J backbones. Compare ROME, MEMIT, MEND, constrained fine-tuning, and at least one parameter-free or parameter-preserving method such as IKE or SERAC. Apply edits cumulatively with no rollback at edit counts such as 1, 10, 100, and 1000, filtering out facts the base model cannot recall. After each edit block, measure Reliability on edited prompts, Generalization on paraphrases, Locality on out-of-scope prompts, COUNTERFACT ES/PS/NS, held-out factual recall, perplexity on LAMBADA, and unrelated-task performance on HellaSwag and Natural Questions. Verify parameter-free methods by hashing base model weights before and after inference and reporting any extra memory or retrieval parameters separately. If parameter editors preserve high Reliability and Generalization while maintaining Locality, perplexity, and unrelated-task accuracy across hundreds or thousands of cumulative edits, the main claim is weakened. If single-edit results are strong but locality, fluency, factual recall, or downstream task performance degrades as edits accumulate, the claim is supported. If parameter-free methods achieve comparable edit success with less degradation and unchanged weight hashes, that supports the claim that they are a serious alternative rather than a fallback. This experiment could be made unnecessary by existing public logs that already report cumulative no-rollback editing across these datasets, methods, backbones, and unrelated capability benchmarks.

To address subclaim Do the near-perfect editing results reported in prior work survive realistic evaluation?, reproduce the headline single-edit COUNTERFACT and ZSRE results for ROME, MEMIT, and MEND under their original evaluation settings, then rerun them under stricter but standard controls: multiple prompt templates, paraphrase and equivalent-neighborhood probes, portability probes such as subject replacement and one-hop questions, out-of-scope locality prompts, base-model recall filtering, generated-prompt validation, and cross-backbone replication on GPT-2 and GPT-J. Include pre-edit, fine-tuning, and in-context IKE baselines. Report how much ES/PS/NS, Reliability, Generalization, and Locality change between the original and stricter settings. If near-perfect scores persist under paraphrases, portability, validated prompts, and cross-model replication without locality loss, the subclaim is weakened. If scores collapse mainly on paraphrase, portability, or locality while original canonical-prompt efficacy remains high, this supports the claim that earlier near-perfect results did not survive realistic evaluation. This experiment could be made unnecessary if prior work has already released complete per-example predictions under both original and stricter prompt/locality/portability evaluations.

To address subclaim Are localized weight edits disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space?, perform a geometric mechanism study on GPT-2 and GPT-J using COUNTERFACT edits from ROME and MEMIT. For each layer, estimate the covariance spectrum of hidden states from a large public text sample such as WikiText-103 or C4 validation, then decompose each edit-induced activation change into principal-component directions. Measure whether the ratio of post-edit activation displacement to weight-update norm is larger in low-variance eigendirections than in high-variance directions, and whether low-variance displacement predicts global side effects such as out-of-scope prediction changes, perplexity increases, or drops on HellaSwag/LAMBADA. Add layer and token-position sweeps, causal tracing and representation-zeroing localization variants, and regression controls for layer identity so the result is not just an edit-layer artifact. If low-variance projections are disproportionately amplified and predict downstream locality or capability damage, this supports the geometric limitation claim. If amplification is uniform across the spectrum or unrelated to damage after controlling for layer and edit size, the geometric explanation is weakened even if editing damage exists. This experiment could be made unnecessary by released activation-difference traces and covariance-spectrum analyses linking edit direction, amplification, and locality damage across multiple editors and models.
reference_experiments: Fix the measurement floor and the inference protocol before editing anything. Score the unedited model on the editing benchmark to establish the pre-edit baseline, and re-run single-edit evaluation of existing methods under plain autoregressive decoding rather than the teacher-forced protocol prior work used, since teacher forcing supplies the ground-truth answer tokens at inference and inflates every number. If methods keep their near-perfect single-edit scores under honest decoding there is no discrepancy to explain. The authors report a pre-edit baseline of Reliability 3.00, Generalization 3.00, Locality 15.50, Portability 4.36 on ZsRE, and a best parameter-based single-edit average of 25.99.

Validate the scoring instrument before quoting any number from it. Judge semantic consistency of generated answers with a strong LLM across reliability, generalization, locality and portability, then cross-check that ranking with a deterministic token-level measure (match ratio and exact match) that does not depend on a model's opinion. If the two disagree, every result is an artifact of the judge rather than a property of the editing methods. The authors find the token-level check reproduces the semantic ranking, with the pre-edit model at 100% by definition and GRACE holding 100% under both single and sequential editing.

Test the asserted mechanism directly. Take the SVD of the original hidden-representation matrix, compute the directional relative change rate R_k = sqrt(n)|u_k^T delta_h| / sigma_k for each principal direction after an edit, and check where amplification concentrates and how it behaves as edits accumulate. The claim's causal story requires R_k > 1 predominantly in low-singular-value directions with the fraction rising monotonically with edit count, across methods and architectures.

Run the main benchmark. Compare eleven editing methods spanning locate-then-edit (ROME, MEMIT, PMET, RECT, AlphaEdit, FT-L), meta-learning (MEND), additional-parameter (AdaLoRA, WISE) and external-memory (GRACE, SCR) families, under sequential editing at 1, 10, 100 and full-dataset edit counts, on ZsRE and WikiData-counterfact, across Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, reporting all four dimensions. The claim holds if every parameter-modifying method degrades toward zero as edits accumulate and the parameter-free retrieval baseline outscores all of them; the authors report ROME, RECT, FT-L, MEND and AdaLoRA at 0.00-0.25 average under sequential editing on DeepSeek-R1-Distill, against SCR at 56.59 single and 60.19 sequential.

Measure damage to capabilities the edits never targeted. Take the models edited in the main benchmark and evaluate them on mathematical reasoning (AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH-500) and broad benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, ARC-c, MMLU-Pro), reporting accuracy after 10 and after 100 sequential edits. Without this the study would only show editing is ineffective, not that it is damaging. The authors report ROME and RECT losing 2.74 and 8.37 average accuracy at 10 edits and falling to near zero at 100, with MEND at 0.00 after both.

Rule out that the result is an artifact of scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty or one method's configuration. Repeat the sweep on larger models (Llama-2-13B, Qwen3-14B), on event-level knowledge (ELKEN, with events converted to triples for the parameter-based arms), split by high- and low-confidence fact sets, and probe the hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity of AlphaEdit — the one method that does not collapse — including its failure to run on Llama-2 and Mistral. If the collapse disappears at 13-14B or only occurs on triple-shaped facts, the claim is bounded rather than general.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A clean pre-edit control and an inference protocol that evaluates generated answers without supplying the reference answer tokens, allowing single-edit results to be compared against the inflated prior protocol.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 includes pre-edit controls and a rerun under stricter realistic evaluation, while proposed experiment 0 includes edit count 1 within a realistic cumulative benchmark and evaluates generated-task outcomes. Together they would establish baseline performance and whether apparent single-edit efficacy survives ordinary inference rather than teacher forcing.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An independent, deterministic answer-level measurement that cross-checks semantic judging and can reveal whether the reported method ranking is an artifact of the evaluator.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set reports several editing and task metrics, but it never specifies an independent token-level match/exact-match check against the semantic consistency scores or a comparison of their rankings.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 1 establishes whether semantic evaluation agrees with a deterministic answer-level measurement.
[2] Agreement or disagreement determines whether the apparent editing ranking is a property of the methods or an artifact of the judge.
[3] Proposed experiments 0 and 1 report efficacy, reliability, generalization, locality, and downstream outcomes but do not perform that cross-modal judge-versus-token check.
[4] A team running the proposed set would therefore not learn whether the headline ranking is evaluator-dependent: missing.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A normalized directional analysis of edit-induced representation changes that tests concentration in low-variance directions, follows that concentration as edits accumulate, and checks that it is reproducible across editing methods and model architectures.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 directly decomposes activation changes in a covariance eigensystem, compares low- and high-variance directions, and relates amplification to global side effects with layer controls. Proposed experiment 0 supplies cumulative edit counts and damage outcomes. However, the proposed set does not explicitly collect the directional geometric statistic at each cumulative edit count or test a monotonic increase in the low-variance fraction, and its direct geometry study is limited to two editors and two GPT-like backbones.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 2 tests not only low-variance amplification but also whether the amplification pattern strengthens monotonically with edit count across methods and architectures.

[2] Proposed experiment 2 measures low-variance amplification and its association with side effects, while proposed experiment 0 measures cumulative damage, but neither specifies directional measurements across the cumulative edit counts.
[3] The proposed geometry study also does not establish that the pattern is independent of the two selected editors and related backbone family.

[4] The team could learn that low-variance displacement occurs and correlates with damage, but would not unambiguously learn that the geometric amplification itself compounds monotonically and is general across parameter-editing methods: partial.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A comparative sequential-edit evaluation that spans parameter-modifying and weight-preserving alternatives, measures edit success and collateral effects, and tests whether those outcomes deteriorate as the number of edits grows.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 directly compares multiple parameter editors with parameter-free or parameter-preserving alternatives over two factual-editing datasets, two backbones, and cumulative counts through 1000, while measuring reliability, generalization, locality, factual recall, fluency, and unrelated-task performance. Proposed experiment 1 adds realistic single-edit and portability/locality checks. The claim does not bind the particular methods, datasets, architectures, or exact number of benchmark dimensions used in the reference, so this supplies comparable discriminating evidence.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Direct post-edit evaluation of capabilities unrelated to the edited facts, at multiple cumulative edit loads, so collateral capability damage can be distinguished from mere failure to perform the edits.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 measures perplexity and performance on unrelated language-understanding and factual-question-answering tasks after each edit block, including the 10- and 100-edit conditions. These are alternative instruments for detecting damage to untargeted capabilities; the claim does not require the reference's particular mathematics and broad-benchmark suite.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence that the observed degradation and geometric mechanism persist across substantially different model scales, knowledge types and fact difficulties, and method configurations rather than being artifacts of one narrow benchmark or implementation.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set varies two backbones, two factual-editing datasets, several editing families, layers, token positions, and geometric controls, so it probes some implementation and architecture dependence. It does not test larger-scale models comparable to the reference sweep, event-level knowledge, explicit high/low-confidence fact splits, or hyperparameter sensitivity of a method that may resist collapse. Those omissions leave important alternative explanations open.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 5 asks whether the result survives changes in scale, knowledge representation, fact difficulty, and configuration.
[2] Proposed experiments 0-2 provide some variation in backbones, datasets, editing methods, layers, and token positions.
[3] They do not include event-level facts, explicit confidence/difficulty strata, larger-scale models, or the targeted hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity analysis.
[4] Consequently, a favorable or unfavorable result could still be specific to small GPT-like models, CounterFact/ZSRE-style facts, or the chosen configurations.
[5] The team would learn that the effect is tested in several setups, but would not resolve the main scale, knowledge-type, difficulty, and configuration confounds: partial.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set directly tests realistic single and sequential editing, collateral capability damage, parameter-free weight preservation, and the central low-variance geometric hypothesis. It would therefore support or weaken the claim in the tested GPT-2/GPT-J and CounterFact/ZSRE scope. It would not fully settle the broad claim as written because the measurement-validity cross-check is absent, the cumulative geometric mechanism is not directly tracked, and robustness to scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty, and configuration remains unresolved.
